doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Benin brass bands, the clave and Dutch Guiana
summary: He explains how the clave originates in Benin brass traditions (Gangbe) and parallels in Dutch Guiana, source of 'Sugar Finger'.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: In Africa, right, B-E-N-I-N. They have a whole brass tradition in Benin. And part of that brass tradition is the origins of the clave because the music they play is [claps] and they didn’t get it from Latin America.

No. It comes from there and the tuba is the bass and the tuba — I went to a concert this brass band Gangbe — G-A-N-G-B-E — Gangbe, a brass band coming from Benin. And it was at Carnegie Hall after hours. And I got there a little late and I heard music coming out of the sound system coming down the escalator and I said why are they playing this Latin band on the Muzak while the band is on stage playing because the bass is going [scats]. I said why are they playing Latin music, and then going [claps rhythm]. And when I went in there it was this band playing and I got this huge Aha. Ahaaaa. They talk about the clave and it’s played in Latin music and everything but all that came from —

And I was reading a book about slavery and where people landed. And in the book it spoke about people from Benin landing all through the Caribbean. All through like down around Cuba and all those islands all through there and down in like the northern part of down in — the people from Holland and the music of Guiana, Dutch Guiana landing

there, which also has a tradition that parallels in so many ways I mean it’s unbelievable, it parallels the whole Dirty Dozen Brass Band type tradition. They have the snare drum separate, they have a bass drum separate, the tuba is the bass, the ensemble looks like the Dirty Dozen but the music that comes out is night and day different. That’s one of the tunes that I recorded called “Sugar Finger.” It comes from Dutch Guiana, it’s a traditional song from Dutch Guiana.

And again they get their instruments from orphanages, from being in the Army band, then they take the instruments and play the traditional music with it. I mean it really parallels New Orleans except it’s about a thousand miles away down in the northern coast of South America.
